item.title: What ZDR Actually Proves After NVIDIA Restricted Frontier Models
item.description:
An enterprise may be willing to let an external model read a piece of code while refusing to let the vendor retain it for a month. These choices are consistent: processing data briefly to complete a task carries different risks from allowing another company to store, correlate, and retrieve it over time.

Reports in September 2026 about NVIDIA restricting frontier models brought this distinction into focus. They do not establish that NVIDIA stopped using Anthropic and OpenAI altogether. They raise a more specific question than which model is strongest: when safety monitoring also requires data, who gets to decide whether that data stays?

Separate reports, announcements, and causes

On September 14, Reuters relayed a report from The Information: NVIDIA was limiting Anthropic models to less sensitive tasks, Palantir was seeking irrevocable zero-data-retention arrangements, and Booz Allen was restricting their use for proprietary cybersecurity work. The report covered enterprise concerns about data at Anthropic and OpenAI, but provided no formal notice of NVIDIA banning both companies’ models across the board. The parties did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Reuters report

A separate, publicly confirmed fact is that NVIDIA and Palantir announced a supply chain intelligence partnership on September 10. The deployment would begin with NVIDIA’s own operations, using Nemotron and emphasizing control of proprietary data. Joint announcement

These developments can be considered together, but they cannot be joined into an unproven causal claim: “NVIDIA switched to Nemotron because of Claude’s retention policy.” Deploying its own models could involve business customization, cost, data governance, and product strategy at the same time. The deployment announcement does not confirm every motive suggested by the reporting.

Nor has NVIDIA always rejected external models. In April, it described its internal use of GPT-5.5-powered Codex, saying that more than 10,000 employees were already using it. The deployment used approved cloud virtual machines, dedicated environments for individual employees, read-only access to production systems, and a ZDR policy. This is the company’s own disclosure, not an independent audit. It nevertheless shows that the question is which paths and data an external model may access. NVIDIA’s deployment account

Why 30 days can change a purchasing decision

On June 9, Anthropic released Fable 5 and Mythos 5, explaining that this class of model required 30-day retention of business traffic to detect complex abuse across interactions. The company said the purpose was safety defense rather than training new Claude models. Launch and retention announcement

For a vendor, an individual request may not reveal an attack assembled from multiple requests. For a customer, retaining the full content creates an additional storage location, access process, and exposure to incidents over the following month. Both sides may be pursuing security while reaching different conclusions about what security requires.

This does not overturn a promise not to use data for training. It shows that the promise never answered every question. Even if data does not change model weights, it may still enter logs, abuse investigations, troubleshooting, or other service state. Whether sensitive designs, unpublished financial information, or supply chain data enter a training set is only one measure of their exposure.

On September 1, Anthropic announced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards. The proposal would store safety signals in customer-controlled cloud storage, with customers managing keys, permissions, and audits. A phased rollout was planned for later that fall, with temporary ZDR arrangements for eligible customers in the meantime. Announcing a solution, establishing a customer’s eligibility, and completing a deployment are three different states. By mid-September, this could not be described as a guarantee already delivered to every customer. EFS announcement

ZDR is not an umbrella for four different promises

Zero data retention is first a service arrangement with a defined scope: which organization, which endpoint, which content, and which retention period. Reducing it to “the vendor never touches data” makes it harder to verify.

Promise What it actually answers What still needs separate confirmation
No use for training Whether inputs and outputs improve the model Safety logs, fault records, and human investigations
Zero data retention Whether the agreed content is stored persistently Covered models, endpoints, data types, and exceptions
Restricted human access Who can view raw content Automated processing, approved exceptions, and access records
Customer-controlled storage Who manages location, keys, and permissions Runtime processing, subcontractors, and the customer’s own configuration risks

OpenAI’s data controls documentation distinguishes training use, abuse monitoring logs, and application state. API data not being used for training by default does not make every feature stateless. Applying for ZDR also requires checking endpoint eligibility: files, conversations, and vector stores do not automatically inherit the same guarantees from the settings of an ordinary request. OpenAI data controls documentation

This distinction matters particularly for agents. An individual call might retain no content, while the agent’s file store, conversation history, tool logs, and third-party search services still hold information. Reviewing only the model endpoint does not cover the entire workflow.

What has counted as evidence that nothing was retained?

A customer cannot tell from a normal response whether the server also saved a log. Capturing network traffic can show what was sent, but cannot reveal everything that happened inside the vendor’s systems. Credible ZDR has therefore depended on mutually consistent evidence, rather than a dashboard displaying a zero.

The contract defines scope and responsibility first: retention periods, permitted uses, subcontractors, exceptions, change notices, and audit rights. Account settings apply these commitments to organizations, projects, models, and APIs. Architecture documentation explains which systems handle the data; operational records show whether access, deletion, and exception procedures followed the agreement. Independent audits provide assurance about particular controls over a specified period.

Verification layer Evidence to obtain Limits of that evidence
Obligations DPA, ZDR agreement, exceptions, and change clauses A basis for accountability, not proof that every call complied
Configuration Organization approval, endpoint eligibility, versions, and retention settings Covers only the paths associated with that configuration
Data flow Log locations, access controls, caching, and deletion mechanisms Must also explain state outside the model and downstream services
Operations Access and deletion records, exception handling, and audit reports Audits have a scope and period; they are not permanent guarantees

A SOC 2 report or ISO certification does not replace this work. An enterprise needs to check whether the report covers the purchased service and relevant controls, rather than merely finding a badge on the vendor’s website. Error logs, caches, and overlooked intermediate services are particularly easy to miss in the gap between a contractual commitment and its implementation.

A model upgrade can reopen the issue. A previously approved model might not require a particular kind of retention, while a new one requires safety review. Automatic switching could then carry the customer beyond its original boundary without a new decision. Irrevocable commitments become a negotiating point because customers want not only today’s configuration, but also the right to refuse when the rules change.

A strict mode should stop when conditions are not met

Zero retention cannot be engineered through a vague intention to log as little as possible. The failure behavior must be explicit: when a model or feature does not satisfy the constraint, is the call rejected, or does the system quietly switch to default retention?

AWS Bedrock’s retention documentation offers a useful implementation example. A strict no-retention mode can block models that require data to be stored; setting store=false in a request does not replace the platform’s retention policy. Supported modes may change, but the design principle is clear: if the constraint is not met, do not proceed with the call. Bedrock retention documentation

Enterprises can design access controls around this principle without depending on every vendor keeping the same rules forever. Public material can go to general services, while restricted data follows approved paths only. Files and tools can be reviewed separately, and model version changes can trigger a new review. The essential requirement is that the list governs real requests, rather than simply appearing in a procurement appendix.

Running one’s own models can shorten the path data takes across organizations, but does not automatically remove risk. Responsibility for keys, patches, permissions, backups, and security response returns to the enterprise. A self-hosted service that nobody maintains may be more vulnerable than a mature vendor’s controlled service.

Questions an enterprise should be able to answer

Instead of asking only whether ZDR is supported, ask the vendor and internal platform team to explain together:

  • Which organization, region, model version, endpoint, and intermediate services handle this call.
  • Where inputs, outputs, metadata, files, caches, and tool logs are stored, and for how long.
  • Which automated systems and people can access them, who approves exceptions, and what evidence is recorded.
  • Who notifies customers when model upgrades or safety policies change, and whether customers can continue to refuse retention.
  • Whether the system rejects the request, alerts the customer, or switches modes when the conditions are no longer met.

This evidence cannot prove absolutely that no copy has ever existed anywhere. It can turn a vague promise into an arrangement that can be checked, declined, and enforced.

Frontier models intensify the conflict: safety systems want to observe usage for longer, while enterprises want raw data to disappear quickly. A purchasing decision therefore depends on more than model intelligence. When both requirements cannot be satisfied, can the enterprise still hold to the boundary it approved?

References

  • Reuters: Report on Palantir, NVIDIA, and Booz Allen restricting model use over data concerns
  • The Information: Anthropic data concerns prompt enterprise restrictions on model use
  • Anthropic: Fable and Mythos access and data retention policy
  • Anthropic: Data retention practices for Covered Models
  • Anthropic: API and data retention
  • Anthropic: Enterprise Frontier Safeguards
  • OpenAI: Platform data controls
  • OpenAI: Security and privacy
  • NVIDIA: Internal deployment of GPT-5.5-powered Codex
  • NVIDIA and Palantir: Sovereign intelligence for critical supply chains
  • AWS Bedrock: Data retention modes

Original Prompt

$blog-writer provides a detailed breakdown of the whole story. Reports indicate that Nvidia has internally restricted the use of frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI, switching sensitive data to its own AI. How did various companies previously prove ZDR?

Rewrite the articles from these three months. If an article was not written by AI, do not rewrite it.

item.title: After the GPT-5.6 Price Reduction, What's the Actual Price Difference Between the Latest Large Model APIs at Home and Abroad
item.description:
The problem with the previous version was not in the calculations, but in sample selection: it picked “representative SKUs,” while users wanted “the latest models from each manufacturer.” Putting the old ERNIE 5.0, GLM-5, Kimi K2.6, and MiniMax M2.7 into a single table labeled “latest prices” made the percentages that followed incomparable.

Only one rule is adopted this time: for each company, only the latest proprietary text model that is publicly available through API is included. OpenAI is an exception that needs to be expanded rather than compressed—GPT-5.6 has three tiers in the same generation: Sol, Terra, and Luna, all of which are available through the API, and Terra alone cannot represent OpenAI as a whole.

First, let’s clarify exactly what was reduced in this “ChatGPT price cut.” On July 30, OpenAI adjusted the standard API price of GPT-5.6 Terra from $2.50 / $15 to $2 / $12, and Luna from $1 / $6 to $0.20 / $1.20; Sol remained unchanged. This is a change in API usage-based pricing, not a discount on ChatGPT/Codex subscription monthly fees. The announcement also clearly states that subscription prices and package quota budgets remain unchanged; only the quota deductions for Terra and Luna in their respective products have been reduced.

A Price List for the Latest Models Only

Synthetic price = 1M uncached input token + 1M output token. Terra’s $2 + $12 = $14, noted as 100%. The RMB quotation uses a fixed exchange rate of $1 = ¥6.7939, used only for sorting; it does not include caching, Batch/Flex/Fast, tool calls, taxes, or enterprise agreement pricing.

Rank Vendor Latest Publicly Available API Model Standard Price (Input / Output, per 1M tokens) Synthesized Price (USD Estimate) Relative to Terra
1 Anthropic Claude Fable 5（2026-06-09） $10 / $50 $60.00 428.6%
2 OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol（2026-07-09） $5 / $30 $35.00 250.0%
3 Moonshot AI Kimi K3 $3 / $15 $18.00 128.6%
4 OpenAI GPT-5.6 Terra（baseline） $2 / $12 $14.00 100.0%
5 Google Gemini 3.6 Flash（2026-07-21 GA） $1.5 / $7.5 $9.00 64.3%
6 xAI Grok 4.5（2026-07-16） $2 / $6 $8.00 57.1%
7 Alibaba Cloud Qwen3.7-Max（2026-06-08 stable snapshot） ¥12 / ¥36 $7.07 50.5%
8 Volcengine Doubao-Seed-Evolving（rolling SKU updates） ¥6 / ¥30 $5.30 37.9%
9 Baidu ERNIE 5.1（input ≤32K） ¥4 / ¥18 $3.24 23.1%
10 MiniMax MiniMax-M3（input ≤512K） ¥2.1 / ¥8.4 $1.55 11.0%
11 OpenAI GPT-5.6 Luna $0.20 / $1.20 $1.40 10.0%
12 DeepSeek DeepSeek-V4-Pro（current public preview flagship） $0.435 / $0.87 $1.31 9.3%
13 Tencent Hy3（Guangzhou region） ¥1 / ¥4 $0.74 5.3%

“Latest” in the table comes in two not-so-neat forms: Doubao-Seed-Evolving is a rolling update under the same model ID, without a fixed release date like a regular version number; DeepSeek-V4-Pro is a preview series for the current public API flagship. They still align better with the table’s standard than historical SKUs that have been replaced by later models.

Models that have an API but are not included in the price ranking
Vendor Latest Public API Model Why Not Calculate a Percentage
Zhipu (Zhipu AI) GLM-5.2 Officially confirmed as the latest flagship with API support, but the publicly crawlable official page does not list per-token pricing; the old pricing of GLM-5.1 cannot be used as a substitute.
Cohere Command A+ Trial and production keys come with limited free usage, while production deployment goes through Model Vault; Cohere has not published per-token pricing that can be compared horizontally with the main table.
Mistral Leanstral 1.5 A free API endpoint is offered, but it is dedicated to Lean 4 formal verification; it is not a $0 pricing for a general-purpose production API and cannot be included in this general task cost table.

This is not an omission—it’s exactly what you encounter when “looking only at the latest”: some new products only offer trial credits first, some are sold exclusively through enterprise channels, and some only provide model descriptions in public materials without listing per-token pricing. Filling the table with previous-generation prices might make it look complete, but it would actually turn the issue from “temporarily not comparable” into an incorrect number.

What This Price Adjustment Means Within OpenAI’s Own Three Tiers

Sol’s composite price is 2.5 times that of Terra (150% higher); Terra is in the middle; Luna is 10% of Terra. Therefore, this price reduction of Terra and Luna does not mean that “flagship models have become cheaper across the board.” Instead, OpenAI has further widened the gap between the mid-tier and low-cost tiers while keeping Sol positioned at the premium price point.

OpenAI’s stated reason is improved inference efficiency: the model, inference system, and the agent layer connecting tools and context are all being optimized. The announcement states that production kernel optimization reduced end-to-end service costs by 20%, and experiments improved token generation efficiency by more than 15%. This is a vendor disclosure that can explain why there is room for price reductions, but it is not a complete cost table available for external audit. As for whether the low price is mainly aimed at competing for high-volume API workloads, it can only be an analysis of the pricing structure, not an official motive.

This Table Is Not a Substitute for Model Selection

Price sorted from expensive to cheap does not mean tasks sorted from good to bad. Long context triggers tiered pricing, and cache hits, reasoning tokens, tool calls, retry counts, region, and enterprise contracts all change the actual bill. The “1M input + 1M output” in the table is only a unified filter before procurement.

When making a real choice, it’s more reliable to test with ten to twenty actual tasks: first look at success rate, latency, and human rework, then record input, output, reasoning tokens, cache hits, and total cost. What you should ultimately compare is the “total cost per successful task,” not an isolated per-unit price on this table.

References

  • OpenAI: GPT-5.6 Release and Three-Tier API Pricing, published on 2026-07-09, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • OpenAI: GPT-5.6 Price-Performance Announcement, published on 2026-07-30, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • OpenAI API: GPT-5.6 Terra Model Page, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • Anthropic: Claude Fable 5, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • Google: Gemini API Changelog and Model Pricing, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • xAI: Grok 4.5 and Pricing Information, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • Alibaba Cloud Bailian: Model Pricing, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • DeepSeek: V4 Release and Pricing Information, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • Zhipu: Latest Model Releases and Model Overview, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • Volcano Engine: Doubao Large Model and Pricing, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • Tencent Cloud: Hy3 Model List and Pricing, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • Baidu: ERNIE 5.1 Release and Qianfan Model Service Pricing, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • Moonshot AI: Kimi Open Platform, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • MiniMax: Pay-As-You-Go Pricing, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • Cohere: Command A+, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • Mistral: Leanstral 1.5, accessed: 2026-07-31.
  • Bank of China: Foreign Exchange Quotation, using the USD spot exchange selling rate on 2026-07-24, accessed: 2026-07-31.
写作附记

Writing Instructions

This article is a snapshot of public API list prices as of 2026-07-31 and does not constitute advice on procurement, investment, or product selection. It only includes verified vendors and does not represent an exhaustive list of all API providers worldwide; model capabilities, tokenizers, context, caching, inference tokens, tool charges, regions, and enterprise contracts vary, and the percentages in the table should not be treated as equivalent performance or actual task cost rankings.

Original Prompt

ChatGPT’s series of models have officially announced price reductions. Let’s organize the relevant information: why are they cutting prices? Compile the API prices of major model providers, both domestic and international, into a table. Using ChatGPT 5.6 terra as the baseline, calculate the price comparison percentages of each provider in the table, sorted from most expensive to cheapest.

The compiled table information is incomplete—other ChatGPT models aren’t listed, and the models from major providers aren’t the latest released ones. I only need the latest model prices from each provider.

item.title: Big Tech Dominance in the U.S. Stock Market Intensifies: The Top 10 Companies Account for 40% of Market Capitalization, Is AI a Bubble or a Revolution?
item.description:
• Analysis of NVIDIA’s “Play” Worth a Billion Investment The global capital market is witnessing an unprecedented wave of centralization in 2025, centered around artificial intelligence (AI). This narrative not only reshapes the tech industry’s landscape but also exacerbates wealth inequality on Wall Street. The former “Magnificent Seven” no longer adequately describes today’s dynamics; the market is now dominated by a handful of super winners.

This article will delve into three key questions:

  1. What proportion of the entire stock market do the top ten U.S. companies represent in terms of market capitalization?
  2. Does AI constitute a bubble? Is NVIDIA’s (NVIDIA) multi-billion dollar “reciprocal investment” with OpenAI justified?
  3. What are NVIDIA’s recent investment moves, and what is the underlying strategic logic behind them?

Write article: What proportion of the entire stock market do the top ten U.S. companies represent? Does AI constitute a bubble? Are NVIDIA’s investments and reciprocal investment with OpenAI justified? Compile NVIDIA’s recent investment actions and analyze their rationale.

Market Concentration: Top 10 Giants Dominate 40% of US Stock Market Capitalization

Based on the latest data from October to November 2025, the concentration in the US stock market (represented by the S&P 500 Index) has reached a remarkable level.

The top 10 US companies in the S&P 500 currently account for approximately 40% of the index’s total market capitalization.

This figure represents an even greater increase than the roughly 30% held by the “Big Seven” a year or two ago. As of early November 2025, the top 10 US companies were approximately:

  1. NVIDIA: Market Cap Approaching $5 Trillion
  2. Apple: Market Cap Approximately $4 Trillion
  3. Microsoft: Market Cap Approximately $3.85 Trillion
  4. Alphabet (Google): Market Cap Approximately $3.4 Trillion
  5. Amazon: Market Cap Approximately $2.6 Trillion
  6. Broadcom: Market Cap Approximately $1.75 Trillion
  7. Meta Platforms: Market Cap Approximately $1.63 Trillion
  8. Tesla: Market Cap Approximately $1.52 Trillion
  9. Berkshire Hathaway: Market Cap Approximately $1.03 Trillion
  10. JPMorgan Chase: Market Cap Approximately $0.85 Trillion

This high concentration means that the stock price performance of a few key companies can determine the entire market’s direction. And the core fuel driving this “super-concentration” is, without question – Artificial Intelligence.

AI Bubble and the $100 Billion “Closed Loop”: NVIDIA’s “Mutual Investment” with OpenAI

The “mutual investment” between NVIDIA and OpenAI, which you mentioned, became a global shock event by September 2025. This wasn’t traditional VC investment, but a strategic partnership valued at $100 billion, representing a significant shift in the AI landscape.

1. The “Closed Loop” Structure of the Partnership:

  • NVIDIA Investment: NVIDIA announced it would invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI.
  • OpenAI Procurement: OpenAI will utilize this funding (and other financing) to purchase NVIDIA’s chip systems, committing to deploy at least 10 ExaWatts (EW) of computing power – involving millions of GPUs – and adopting NVIDIA’s next-generation “Vera Rubin” platform starting in 2026.

2. Is This Model Reasonable?

This is a highly controversial topic, with market opinions divided between “revolution” and “bubble.”

Perspective 1: Reasonable - It’s the Inevitable Choice of the ‘AI Revolution’ (The Revolution Case)

  • For OpenAI (the Buyer): The path to Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) requires near-unlimited computing power. In today’s market, NVIDIA’s GPUs are the most powerful and have the most mature ecosystems – they are the “shovels.” Locking down supply of top-tier chips for several years is the only way to ensure its continued leadership in the AI arms race.
  • For NVIDIA (the Seller): OpenAI is its largest and most important customer. By investing $100 billion and deeply binding itself with OpenAI, NVIDIA effectively secures a massive order for its next-generation platform (Vera Rubin), guaranteeing future revenue and absolute market dominance over several years.

Perspective 2: Unreasonable - It’s a Classic ‘AI Bubble’ Feature (The Bubble Case)

  • “Closed Loop Financing”: Critics argue this is a “left hand, right hand” capital game. NVIDIA gives money to OpenAI, which then uses that money to order from NVIDIA. This creates massive revenue and growth on paper, but significantly amplifies valuations and bubbles.
  • Significant Financial Risk: Reports indicate NVIDIA was even discussing providing OpenAI with loan guarantees to build data centers. This means if OpenAI’s business model fails in the future (e.g., AGI doesn’t materialize or operating costs are too high leading to bankruptcy), NVIDIA faces risks of tens of billions – or even hundreds of billions – in debt.
  • Raises Antitrust Concerns: This transaction is viewed by regulators and competitors as “anti-competitive.” Analysts worry that, as a market “arms dealer,” NVIDIA will use its investment to deeply bind itself with the largest “mercenary” OpenAI, incentivizing it to refuse selling chips to OpenAI’s competitors (like Anthropic, Google, etc.), or offer worse terms, thereby stifling innovation.

Conclusion: This model is NVIDIA’s high-risk, high-reward strategic “play” to ensure its AI dominance. It’s both a catalyst for massive AI development and potentially the footnote on the largest bubble in history.

Nvidia’s Investment “Empire”: A Calculated Demand Creation

Nvidia has long been more than just a “chip vendor.” Through its venture capital arm (NVIDIA GPU Ventures), it is actively transforming into the “banker” and “ecosystem builder” for the entire AI gold rush.

📈 NVIDIA’s Recent Key Investment Actions

NVIDIA’s investment pace has accelerated dramatically in 2024-2025. As of October 2025, NVIDIA has invested in 59 AI startups this year, surpassing the 55 invested in throughout 2024.

Its investment portfolio covers almost every vertical within AI, with a focus on:

  1. OpenAI (Foundation Models): In September 2025, it reached a strategic investment and procurement agreement valued at $100 billion.
  2. Poolside (AI Programming): Revealed to lead an investment of up to $100 million, supporting the development of AI software engineers in October 2025.
  3. Nokia (6G/Telecoms): Announced a strategic partnership and invested $100 million jointly developing AI-RAN (Radio Access Network) to capture the 6G market.
  4. Figure AI (Humanoid Robots): Investing in this star robotics company, positioning itself for the future of “Embodied Intelligence.”
  5. Perplexity AI (AI Search): Investing in this OpenAI competitor, securing a foothold in the next-generation information gateway.
  6. Wayve (Autonomous Driving): Investing in the UK’s autonomous driving company to ensure its dominance in automotive chips.

🤔 Investment Logic Analysis: Why is it Reasonable?

Nvidia CEO Huang Renjun’s strategy is very clear. The core logic of its investments isn’t purely financial returns, but rather to serve its core chip business, which can be summarized into three key objectives:

1. Core Objective: “Invest, Then Buy My Chips”

This is Nvidia’s most direct investment logic. Nvidia injects capital into startups (like Poolside), who in turn use this money to purchase Nvidia’s expensive GB300 or next-generation GPUs. This not only locks in customers but also artificially creates demand, forming a “mutually beneficial” business ecosystem between Nvidia and its invested companies.

2. Strategic Objective: Building a “CUDA Ecosystem Moat”

Nvidia’s true moat is its CUDA software platform. By scattering money across all levels of the AI ecosystem (robotics, biopharmaceuticals, autonomous driving, AI programming), Nvidia ensures that these most promising future companies develop from day one based on the CUDA platform. This prevents competitors (like AMD, Intel) from shaking Nvidia’s position even if their hardware keeps up in terms of performance – they simply can’t disrupt Nvidia’s dominance in the software ecosystem.

3. Expansion Objective: Securing New Tracks for Chips

Nvidia needs to constantly find the next “AI wave” to support its $500 billion valuation. Its investment in Nokia (6G) is to push its AI chips into the massive telecommunications infrastructure market; its investment in Figure AI (robotics) is a bet on “embodied intelligence” becoming the next major consumer of computing power after cloud computing.

Summary: “Trickery” Under Monopoly

The unprecedented concentration in the US stock market reflects the productivity leap brought about by the AI revolution, but it also carries enormous risks of bubbles. The billion-dollar “closed loop” partnership between Nvidia and OpenAI is a microcosm of this high-stakes gamble.

Nvidia’s investment strategy is a meticulously planned “trickery”: It leverages its strong capital strength to not only become a “weapons supplier” in the AI era, but also to transform into a “banker” and “rule maker,” ensuring that all paths to the future are paved with Nvidia chips. This strategy is highly rational and efficient from a business perspective, but it also exposes it to significant antitrust pressure and potential financial risks.

For investors, understanding this game driven by AI, led by giants, and strengthened by capital closed loops is key to comprehending the current market.
